blocks.body:
What is $\dfrac{\sqrt{x + 9} - 3}{x}$ at $x = 0$? Substituting gives $\tfrac00$, which means nothing. Yet for $x$ near $0$ the values crowd around one number. That number is the limit: not the value at the point, but the value the function is heading for.

Slopes, instantaneous speeds and areas under curves are all limits. This lesson starts with tables, gives the precise definition, and ends with $\sin x / x \to 1$.

blocks.title: Watching values approach
blocks.body:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 9} - 3}{x}$ for $x \ge -9$, $x \ne 0$. Near $0$, to five decimals:
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & -0.1 & -0.01 & -0.001 & 0.001 & 0.01 & 0.1 \\ \hline f(x) & 0.16713 & 0.16671 & 0.16667 & 0.16666 & 0.16662 & 0.16621 \end{array}$$
From both sides the values approach $0.1666\ldots = \tfrac16$. Algebra confirms this: multiplying top and bottom by $\sqrt{x + 9} + 3$,
$$f(x) = \frac{(x + 9) - 9}{x\big(\sqrt{x + 9} + 3\big)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 9} + 3} \qquad (x \ne 0),$$
and as $x$ approaches $0$ the right side approaches $\tfrac{1}{3 + 3} = \tfrac16$. We write $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x) = \tfrac16$.

Note that $f$ is not defined at $0$, and that does not matter: the limit looks at $x$ near $0$, never at $0$ itself. Changing or removing the value at $0$ never changes the limit.

blocks.title: When there is no limit
blocks.body:
A limit must be a single number, approached from both sides. Three things can go wrong.

1. A jump. $s(x) = |x|/x$ is $1$ for $x > 0$ and $-1$ for $x < 0$. The one-sided limits are $\lim_{x\to 0^+} s(x) = 1$ and $\lim_{x\to 0^-} s(x) = -1$; since they differ, $\lim_{x\to 0} s(x)$ does not exist.
2. Blowing up. As $x \to 0$, $1/x^2$ grows beyond every bound. The notation $\lim_{x\to 0} 1/x^2 = \infty$ is shorthand for this way of failing; $\infty$ is not a number.
3. Oscillation. On every interval $(0, \delta)$, $1/x$ runs through infinitely many periods of the sine, so $\sin(1/x)$ takes every value in $[-1, 1]$ there. It approaches nothing.

blocks.title: Limit
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be defined on an open interval around $a$, except possibly at $a$ itself. We say that $f(x)$ tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $a$, and write $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$, if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that
$$0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.$$
In words: however small a tolerance $\varepsilon$ you demand around $L$, every $x$ close enough to $a$ (within $\delta$, but not equal to $a$) gives a value within that tolerance.

blocks.title: The definition as a game
blocks.body:
Think of a game. An opponent names a tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$, as small as they like; you reply with a $\delta > 0$ such that every $x$ with $0 < |x - a| < \delta$ has $f(x)$ within $\varepsilon$ of $L$. The limit is $L$ if you can always reply. Your $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, but not on $x$.

For $\lim_{x\to 3}(2x + 1) = 7$: since $|(2x + 1) - 7| = 2|x - 3|$, the reply $\delta = \varepsilon/2$ works.

The condition $0 < |x - a|$ makes the value at $a$ irrelevant. For $s(x) = |x|/x$ and any $L$, the tolerance $\varepsilon = 1$ cannot be met: every window around $0$ contains points where $s = 1$ and points where $s = -1$, and no number is within $1$ of both.

blocks.title: Limit laws
blocks.body:
Suppose $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = M$. Then
$$\lim_{x\to a}\big(f(x) + g(x)\big) = L + M, \qquad \lim_{x\to a} f(x)g(x) = LM,$$
and, if $M \ne 0$, $\lim_{x\to a} \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{L}{M}$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
All windows are of the form $0 < |x - a| < \delta$; to meet several conditions at once, take the smallest of the corresponding $\delta$'s.

Sum. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose a window in which $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon/2$ and $|g(x) - M| < \varepsilon/2$. There, by the triangle inequality,
$$|f(x) + g(x) - (L + M)| \le |f(x) - L| + |g(x) - M| < \varepsilon.$$

Product. Write $$f(x)g(x) - LM = f(x)\big(g(x) - M\big) + M\big(f(x) - L\big)$$. Using the tolerance $1$ for $f$, there is a window in which $|f(x) - L| < 1$, so $|f(x)| < |L| + 1$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, shrink the window so that also $|g(x) - M| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2(|L| + 1)}$ and $|f(x) - L| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2(|M| + 1)}$. Then
$$|f(x)g(x) - LM| \le |f(x)|\,|g(x) - M| + |M|\,|f(x) - L| < \frac\varepsilon2 + \frac\varepsilon2 = \varepsilon.$$

Quotient. By the product law it is enough to show $1/g(x) \to 1/M$. In a window where $|g(x) - M| < |M|/2$ we have $|g(x)| > |M|/2$ (so $g(x) \ne 0$) and
$$\left|\frac{1}{g(x)} - \frac1M\right| = \frac{|M - g(x)|}{|g(x)|\,|M|} < \frac{2|g(x) - M|}{M^2},$$
which is less than $\varepsilon$ once also $|g(x) - M| < \varepsilon M^2/2$.

blocks.title: Using the laws, and limits at infinity
blocks.body:
From $\lim_{x\to a} c = c$ and $\lim_{x\to a} x = a$, the laws give $\lim_{x\to a} P(x) = P(a)$ for every polynomial $P$, and the same for a quotient of polynomials whose denominator is not $0$ at $a$. When top and bottom both tend to $0$ the laws do not apply directly; simplify first, as above.

$\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ with $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $x > N$. The basic example is $1/x \to 0$ (take $N = 1/\varepsilon$), and the limit laws hold here too. For instance, dividing top and bottom by $x^2$,
$$\frac{3x^2 + 1}{x^2 - 5x} = \frac{3 + 1/x^2}{1 - 5/x} \to \frac{3 + 0}{1 - 0} = 3 \qquad (x \to \infty).$$

blocks.title: Squeeze theorem
blocks.body: Suppose $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ for all $x$ in some window $0 < |x - a| < r$, and $\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = \lim_{x\to a} h(x) = L$. Then $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\delta \le r$ so small that $|g(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ and $|h(x) - L| < \varepsilon$ whenever $0 < |x - a| < \delta$. For such $x$,
$$L - \varepsilon < g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x) < L + \varepsilon,$$
so $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$.

blocks.title: A proof from the definition
blocks.body: Prove from the definition that $\lim_{x\to 2} x^2 = 4$.
blocks.solution:
We need $|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2|\,|x + 2|$ to be small. We control $|x - 2|$; the danger is that $|x + 2|$ might be large. So first restrict to $|x - 2| < 1$: then $1 < x < 3$ and $|x + 2| < 5$.

Given $\varepsilon > 0$, let $\delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/5)$. If $0 < |x - 2| < \delta$, then $|x + 2| < 5$ (as $\delta \le 1$) and $|x - 2| < \varepsilon/5$, so
$$|x^2 - 4| = |x - 2|\,|x + 2| < \frac\varepsilon5 \cdot 5 = \varepsilon.$$
(For $\varepsilon = 0.01$, $\delta = 0.002$, and indeed $2.002^2 = 4.008004$.) Taking a minimum is the standard way to impose two requirements on $\delta$.

blocks.title: Simplify first
blocks.solution:
For the first, since $x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)$, for $x \ne 2$ the quotient equals $x^2 + 2x + 4$, which tends to $12$.

For the second, multiply and divide by $\sqrt{x^2 + x} + x$: for $x > 0$,
$$\sqrt{x^2 + x} - x = \frac{(x^2 + x) - x^2}{\sqrt{x^2 + x} + x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 1/x} + 1} \to \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac12.$$
(At $x = 100$ it is $0.49876\ldots$.) The tempting guess "$\sqrt{x^2 + x} \approx x$, so the limit is $0$" is wrong.

blocks.title: The limit of sin x over x
blocks.body: Prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, with $x$ in radians. Deduce $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac12$.
blocks.solution:
This uses the unit-circle definitions of $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ and the double-angle formula, all from [[trig]].

Take first $0 < x < \pi/2$. On the unit circle with centre $O$, let $A = (1, 0)$, $P = (\cos x, \sin x)$ and $T = (1, \tan x)$, the point where line $OP$ meets the vertical through $A$. The triangle $OAP$ lies inside the circular sector $OAP$, which lies inside the triangle $OAT$. Comparing areas (the sector is the fraction $\tfrac{x}{2\pi}$ of a disc of area $\pi$),
$$\frac12\sin x < \frac12 x < \frac12\tan x.$$
The first inequality gives $\sin x < x$. The second, multiplied by $2\cos x / x > 0$, gives $\cos x < \dfrac{\sin x}{x}$. For a lower bound on $\cos x$, use $1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\frac x2$ and $\sin\frac x2 < \frac x2$:
$$1 - \cos x = 2\sin^2\frac x2 < 2\left(\frac x2\right)^2 = \frac{x^2}{2}.$$
Altogether
$$1 - \frac{x^2}{2} < \cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1 \qquad (0 < x < \tfrac\pi2).$$
Every term is unchanged when $x$ is replaced by $-x$, so this holds for $0 < |x| < \tfrac\pi2$, and the squeeze theorem gives $\sin x / x \to 1$.

For the second limit,
$$\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \frac12\left(\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2 \to \frac12 \cdot 1^2 = \frac12,$$
by the product law and the first limit with $x/2$ in place of $x$.

blocks.title: A function with only one limit
blocks.body: Let $f(x) = x$ when $x$ is rational and $f(x) = 0$ when $x$ is irrational. Show that $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x) = 0$, but that $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ does not exist for any $a \ne 0$.
blocks.solution:
For every $x$, $-|x| \le f(x) \le |x|$, and both bounds tend to $0$, so $f(x) \to 0$ as $x \to 0$ by the squeeze theorem.

Now let $a \ne 0$, suppose $f(x) \to L$ as $x \to a$, and take $\varepsilon = |a|/3$ with its window. Every interval contains rational and irrational numbers ([[real-numbers]]). An irrational $x$ in the window gives $|0 - L| < |a|/3$; a rational $x$ in the window with also $|x - a| < |a|/3$ gives $|x - L| < |a|/3$. Then
$$|a| \le |a - x| + |x - L| + |L| < \frac{|a|}3 + \frac{|a|}3 + \frac{|a|}3 = |a|,$$
which is impossible. So $f$ has a limit at exactly one point.

blocks.body:
- $\tfrac00$ is not automatically $1$: $\tfrac{2x}{x} \to 2$, $\tfrac{x^2}{x} \to 0$, and $\tfrac{x}{x^2}$ has no limit as $x \to 0$, though all three have this form.
- Tables can mislead: $\sin(\pi/x)$ is $0$ at $x = 1, 0.1, 0.01, \ldots$, yet has no limit at $0$.
- "Gets closer and closer" is not the definition: as $x \to 0$, $x^2$ gets ever closer to $-1$, but its limit is $0$.
- The limit laws need both limits to exist: $\sin(1/x) + \big(-\sin(1/x)\big) \to 0$, although neither term has a limit at $0$.

A function whose limit at $a$ equals its value there is continuous ([[continuity]]). The derivative is the limit $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$ ([[derivative]]), and the area under a curve is a limit of sums of rectangles ([[riemann-integral]]). Many $\tfrac00$ limits yield to [[lhopital]], and growth rates as $x \to \infty$ are compared in [[asymptotics]].

Restricting $x$ to the integers gives limits of sequences ([[seq-limits]]) and [[series]]; the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem are limit statements ([[limit-theorems]]).

1. Compute $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{x^2 + x - 2}{x^2 - 1}$.
2. Prove from the definition that $\lim_{x\to 4}\sqrt x = 2$. (Hint: $\sqrt x - 2 = \frac{x - 4}{\sqrt x + 2}$.)
3. Compute $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin 3x}{x}$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\tan x}{x}$.
4. Does $\lim_{x\to 0} x\sin(1/x)$ exist? Justify your answer.

sources.ref: Courant & John, Introduction to Calculus and Analysis, Volume I
